question: How does plucking change the rhythm of a string quartet?
intro: The scherzo sets short, plucked sounds against lines sustained with the bow. A slower middle section reshapes the opening material before the brisk character returns.

sections.label: Slower middle · approximate
sections.mNote: opening motifs expanded slowly, viola-led, with all four instruments muted

relations.label: The plucked scherzo returns
relations.basis: The shortened A′ section restores the opening scherzo after the muted middle. The measured pair agrees with the return marked near 290 s; the identity and plucked scoring come from the form and listening notes, not from chroma. CENS diagonal mean 0.942, sustained 19 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 290 s (cache/form/ravel-quartet-scherzo.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: A note’s beginning matters
cues.text: Pizzicato means plucking a string rather than drawing a bow across it. In this movement, compare the rhythm made by those short attacks with the line of a longer, bowed phrase. A change of technique can alter the character without adding another player.
cues.evidence: Stephen Walsh’s quartet note describes the plucked first theme and bowed second theme. This is a movement-wide listening guide, not a timed identification of a bow change: https://www.chambermusicsociety.org/about-the-music/compositions/ravel-string-quartet
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A line or a set of points?
cues.text: Try hearing the music once as a sequence of separate attacks, then as a phrase joining them together. Which way of listening makes the pulse clearer, and which makes the melody easier to follow?
cues.evidence: The prompt follows the score’s contrast between plucked and bowed material. The audio analysis cannot identify those playing techniques on its own.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Dedicated to his teacher
cues.text: Ravel completed the quartet in April 1903 and dedicated it to Gabriel Fauré. He had joined Fauré’s composition class in 1897 and continued attending as an auditor after losing his formal place at the Conservatoire.
cues.evidence: Stephen Walsh gives the completion date, dedication and Conservatoire history in the Chamber Music Society note: https://www.chambermusicsociety.org/about-the-music/compositions/ravel-string-quartet

cues.title: A slower view of familiar material
cues.text: The middle section takes a slower look at motifs from the opening. Listen for familiar shapes with more space around them; the contrast need not mean that every earlier idea has disappeared.
cues.evidence: Walsh describes the middle as a slow meditation on the opening motifs, still using both plucked and bowed writing. Fewer detected attacks from about 1:40 support this provisional location: https://www.chambermusicsociety.org/about-the-music/compositions/ravel-string-quartet
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Paris, March 1904
cues.text: The Heymann Quartet gave the first performance on 5 March 1904 at a Société nationale de musique concert in Paris. This remained Ravel’s only string quartet.
cues.evidence: The Chamber Music Society note identifies the date, ensemble, venue context and the work’s place in Ravel’s output: https://www.chambermusicsociety.org/about-the-music/compositions/ravel-string-quartet

cues.title: What moves during a long note?
cues.text: In the more sustained stretches, listen below and around the line that holds your attention. Does the surrounding sound change while that line seems to remain still?
cues.evidence: The middle region contains extended spans with few detected new attacks, including around 2:30–3:15. The analysis supports a sustained texture, not a claim about which instrument holds a note.

cues.title: Motion gathers in stages
cues.text: Follow the shorter gestures as activity begins to gather again. Notice whether the sense of motion returns all at once or develops across several phrases.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks become more frequent over the broad span from about 3:20 to 3:45. This cue describes the increase without assigning it to a particular playing technique.

cues.title: Busy need not mean loud
cues.text: Listen to the spacing of the notes as well as their weight. Quick, close attacks can restore rhythmic energy before the sound itself becomes much stronger.
cues.evidence: The analysis finds increased attack activity around 4:30–4:35 while the recorded level remains relatively low; a larger rise in level follows around 4:50.

cues.title: Recognising the scherzo again
cues.text: Compare the restored brisk character with the opening. Listen for the relationship between short attacks and a continuing line, rather than expecting every earlier phrase to return at its original length.
cues.evidence: The score commentary describes a return of the opening section after the slower middle. The renewed activity and level around 4:50 guide this provisional placement; they do not identify a precise thematic entrance: https://www.chambermusicsociety.org/about-the-music/compositions/ravel-string-quartet
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Spacing the ending
cues.text: Follow the closing gestures into the spaces between them. How does the ending distinguish the last few attacks from the continuous activity that came before?
cues.evidence: The feature report shows fewer detected attacks and a lower recorded level across the final fifteen seconds. It does not establish the exact final stroke or its playing technique.

transitions.title: The scherzo’s shapes acquire a longer breath
transitions.how: Ravel slows the motion and puts mutes on all four instruments. A viola-led melodic line expands the scherzo’s material instead of introducing an unrelated trio tune; the rising-fifth shape remains a connection across the change. Plucked and bowed sounds both survive, but longer notes and softer resonance alter their balance. The opening’s A-minor, Aeolian colour gives way to a middle that ranges through other minor keys, including E minor and G♯ minor, rather than settling into a conventional relative-major contrast.
transitions.evidence: The 1:42 section boundary coincides with a quiet region near −29 dB and very few detected attacks after 1:45. Stephen Walsh’s Chamber Music Society note identifies the middle’s all-player mutes, retention of plucked and bowed techniques and meditation on the opening motifs. The structural account at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_Quartet_(Ravel) identifies the viola-led line and minor-key range. These are passage-level score facts, not a pitch-estimate-derived modulation at 1:42.

transitions.title: Plucked attacks recover the opening’s balance
transitions.how: Short figures have already begun to restore motion before the scherzo returns. Ravel brings back its crisp pizzicato theme and A-centred bass, recovering the opening’s two-against-three rhythmic friction after the middle’s more sustained phrases. The familiar rising fifth now belongs to a quick gesture again rather than a broad melodic span. This is a shortened, varied return, not a complete replay: recognition depends on the attack, bass reference and motif arriving together, with the bowed line again set against plucked activity.
transitions.evidence: The 4:50 section boundary brings a level rise from about −23.2 dB at 4:45 to −11.7 dB at 4:50, after attack activity had already increased around 4:30. The form relation matches 0:02.5–0:21.5 with 4:52.5–5:11.5 as a varied return. Walsh’s score commentary supplies the pizzicato/arco contrast and shared rising-fifth motif; the measurements do not independently identify playing techniques.

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
